chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from the one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Everyone who brings a sacrificial animal voluntarily, and his sacrificial animal gets exhausted, so there is nothing upon him. He should slaughter it, and he should take the rein of the yoke, so he should immerse it in the blood, and he should strike its hump with it, and there would not be a replacement upon him.
And whatever was from the penalty of the hunting, or a vow, and it gets exhausted, so it would be upon the like of that, and upon him would be a replacement.
And every thing which enters the Haram and it gets exhausted, so there would be no replacement upon its owner, be it a voluntary one or something else.

key_terms.جَزَاءُ صَيْدٍ: Penalty for hunting game while in Ihram
key_terms.عَطَبَ: To die or become exhausted before reaching the destination
key_terms.نَذْرٌ: A vow or pledge to perform a religious act
key_terms.نَعْلُ التَّقْلِيدِ: The rein or strap used to tie the animal's neck
key_terms.هَدْيٌ: Sacrificial animal brought for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a sacrificial animal dies before reaching the place of sacrifice?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of *hady* (sacrificial animal) loss during transit, distinguishing between voluntary offerings (*tatawwu'*), which incur no penalty, and obligatory vows or hunting penalties (*jaza'*), which require replacement. The ritual marking with the *na'l al-taqilid* (collar ring) dipped in blood serves as a symbolic completion of the obligation even if the animal perishes. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on intent and obligation type in determining liability for ritual losses.
